title: Seoul Street Food Guide 2026: What to Eat, Where & How Much
description: From tteokbokki to hotteok, this is your complete guide to Seoul street food. The best stalls, markets, and food streets — with prices.
content:
Seoul's street food scene is one of the world's great culinary experiences — chaotic, delicious, cheap, and deeply woven into the city's social fabric. Here's where to eat, what to order, and what to pay.

Essential Street Foods

Tteokbokki (떡볶이) — ₩3,000-5,000

The queen of Korean street food. Chewy rice cakes in spicy-sweet gochujang sauce, usually with fish cakes and boiled eggs. Every pojangmacha (street stall) has a different recipe. The best versions have layers of flavor that develop as you eat.

Best at: Sindang-dong Tteokbokki Town (신당동 떡볶이타운)

Hotteok (호떡) — ₩1,500-2,500

Sweet filled pancakes — cinnamon sugar and crushed peanuts inside, crispy outside. Winter comfort food but available year-round. The green tea version at Insadong is exceptional.

Bindaetteok (빈대떡) — ₩5,000-8,000

Mung bean pancakes at Gwangjang Market. Thick, crispy, filling. Eat with the kimchi on the side and a cup of makgeolli (rice wine).

Odeng/Eomuk (어묵) — ₩1,000/skewer

Fish cakes on a skewer, served in hot broth. Perfect winter snack. The broth is always free — drink it from the ladle provided.

Best Street Food Markets

Gwangjang Market (광장시장)

The original. Operating since 1905. The indoor market has hundreds of stalls selling every Korean snack imaginable. Go hungry. Go multiple times.

📍 Metro: Jongno 5-ga, Line 1

Myeongdong Street Food Alley

Touristy but genuinely fun. International flavor combinations (corn dogs with squid, tornado potatoes, dragon's beard candy). Prices slightly higher but portions are generous.

Noryangjin Fish Market (노량진수산물도매시장)

For seafood. Buy your fish/shellfish from the market stalls, then have it prepared at the restaurants upstairs. Incredibly fresh, very affordable.

💡 Money Tip: Most street food vendors prefer cash. Keep small bills (₩1,000, ₩5,000) handy. ATMs are everywhere but card readers are less common at pojangmacha stalls.
